The Yellow-browed melidectes (Melidectes rufocrissalis) displays notable sexual dimorphism in adult body mass, with females reaching an ultimate wet weight of 63.6 grams [Wwi = 63.6 grams]. Field surveys further indicate that female body mass ranges from 56 to 72.7 grams (56-72.7 grams) [Wwi = 56-72.7 grams], a span that likely reflects variation across elevational gradients and seasonal resource availability. Males attain a substantially larger ultimate wet weight of 84.1 grams [Wwi = 84.1 grams], with reported values spanning from 72.7 up to 96.5 grams (72.7-96.5 grams) [Wwi = 72.7-96.5 grams]. At hatching, the neonate emerges at a remarkably modest initial wet weight of just 6.8 grams [Ww0 = 6.8 grams], representing a tiny fraction of adult mass and underscoring the extreme altricial condition typical of many passerines inhabiting montane forests. This minuscule starting mass necessitates a prolonged and intensive period of parental provisioning to fuel the rapid somatic growth required before the chick can achieve independence.

Incubation of the single-egg clutch proceeds under tightly controlled thermal conditions, with the egg developing at a temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C] for a period of 15.5 days [ab = 15.5 days] before hatching. This incubation duration is consistent with values reported for other medium-sized honeyeaters in the region. Following hatching, the nestling chick remains in the nest for a relatively brief developmental period; fledging occurs 15 days after hatching [tx = 15 days after hatching] when maintained at the species' typical active metabolic temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This rapid transition from a fully dependent altricial chick to a fledgling capable of short flights is energetically demanding, reflecting intensive feeding effort by both parents.

The species exhibits a life-history strategy characterized by a slow pace of life relative to its body size. Under the thermal conditions typical of its active metabolic periods, measured at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the age at which individuals attain sexual maturity is 45 days after hatching [tp = 45 days after hatching]. This relatively early onset of reproductive capability is somewhat surprising for a bird reaching such a substantial adult body mass. Furthermore, the first successful breeding event typically occurs at 511 days after hatching [tR = 511 days after hatching] at the same ambient temperature, indicating a delay between physiological readiness and the actual initiation of reproductive activity, likely constrained by the need to establish a breeding territory and secure a mate in the competitive montane environment at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].

Reproductive output is remarkably constrained; each successful nesting attempt yields just a single egg per nest [N_R_i = single egg per nest], and females produce only one such nesting event per year [F_R_i = one such nesting event per year]. This exceptionally low annual fecundity is among the lowest recorded for a passerine of its body size and suggests a strong trade-off between the high energetic costs of chick provisioning and the need for adult survival in a seasonally variable highland habitat. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species, observed under field conditions at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], is approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years], a longevity that allows for repeated, albeit infrequent, breeding attempts over an individual's lifetime, compensating for the low per-event reproductive output.

Basal metabolic rate measurements obtained from respirometry trials conducted at a thermoneutral temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] yielded a resting oxygen consumption of 140 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 140 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This metabolic rate is moderate for a honeyeater of this size and likely reflects an energetic strategy that balances the high costs of thermoregulation in cool montane forests with the need to sustain foraging activity during daylight hours. The modest basal metabolic rate relative to body mass further supports the interpretation of a slow-paced life history, as species with lower mass-specific metabolic demands tend to exhibit delayed reproduction and extended lifespans.
